title: Instructional Illusions: The Magician Will See You Now
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos uses Kirschner, Hendrick and Heal's ten instructional illusions as a lens and proposes an eleventh, the authenticity illusion, applied to Structured Word Inquiry for beginning readers. Her argument is that SWI can look like deep linguistic insight while failing to build the decoding and encoding that produce automatic word recognition. She leans on Share's point that teachers rightly begin with an oversimplified model of the writing system, on Seidenberg's convenient fiction, and on Hendrick's account of complexity built from simplicity. She also explains set for variability as the safeguard that lets students flex pronunciations when a decoding attempt misses. She closes with a call for professional humility about experts, research and uncertainty. It sits in Learning & Curriculum as a pedagogy argument about early reading.
points: Janetos extends the instructional-illusions framework with an authenticity illusion: the belief that early instruction must reflect the full structure of the writing system.
She argues that presenting morphology before the alphabetic principle is secure risks explaining the system rather than giving children a way to access it.
The physics analogy supports the claim that a simplified model is a feature, not a flaw, for novices.
Teaching set for variability from the start answers the worry that one-to-one sound-symbol mapping sets beginners up for later failure.
She asks teachers to tell informed experts from self-interested influencers and to weigh advice against the practical constraints of their own classrooms.
quotes: Presenting the full structure too soon can overwhelm rather than support learning, privileging linguistic completeness over reading competence. What appears more faithful to the structure of English is, in practice, less faithful to the cognitive needs of beginners, which Stanislas Dehaene describes as the mental revolution that is sparked when a child can recognize letters and graphemes and easily turn them into speech sounds.

We don’t want to put the morphological cart before the alphabetic horse regardless of the so-called truth of the writing system. Our goal is to prioritize the truth behind how our brains connect sounds to letters as explained by neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene in Reading in the Brain.

What does a beginning reader gain if they can understand word families (play, plays, played, playing, playful or sign, signal, signature) without being taught an efficient method for how to decode these words in print? The student who can’t decode mat isn’t going to have any more success attempting to read mats, matted, or matting.

The real problem is that SWI can look like powerful instruction while failing to produce the kind of portable learning that transfers to the automatic word recognition we are seeking for our students. Instruction that appears more authentic or faithful to linguistic reality is not necessarily more effective for novices.
Tasking teachers with evaluating expert advice and determining the ‘right’ reasons to accept or reject it is a tall order. But do we have a choice?

Yes, morphology matters, but sound-symbol relationships matter more at the beginning when it comes to laying the foundation for automatic word recognition. Leave the training wheels on the bike until students are so well-balanced that the bumps on the morphological road are manageable.
